verses.text: Agrippa said to Paul, "You may now speak for yourself." So Paul raised his hand and began to defend himself.
"King Agrippa, I am glad that I can stand before you today to answer all the charges the Jews have made against me.
I am especially glad because you know all about Jewish customs and the questions we argue about. So please listen to me patiently.
All the Jews know how I have lived since I was young. They know how I lived from the beginning among my own people and in Jerusalem.
They have known me for a long time. If they want to, they can tell you that I lived as a Pharisee. The Pharisees follow our religion more strictly than any other group.
And now I am on trial because I hope in the promise God made to our ancestors.
Our twelve tribes hope to see this promise come true. That is why they worship God day and night with all their hearts. King Agrippa, it is because of this hope that the Jews accuse me!
Why do any of you think it is impossible for God to raise the dead?
I too once thought that I should do all I could against the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
And that is what I did in Jerusalem. The leading priests gave me power to put many of God's people in prison. When they were put to death, I voted against them.
I often punished them in all the synagogues and tried to force them to speak against God. I was so angry with them that I even went to cities in other countries to attack them.
Once I was on my way to Damascus with the power and orders of the leading priests.
At midday, King Agrippa, as I was on the road, I saw a light from the sky. It was brighter than the sun, and it shone all around me and the men travelling with me.

We all fell to the ground. Then I heard a voice speaking to me in the Hebrew language. It said, 'Saul, Saul, why are you attacking me? You are only hurting yourself by fighting me, like an ox kicking against a sharp stick.'
I asked, 'Who are you, Lord?' The Lord answered, 'I am Jesus, the one you are attacking.
Now get up and stand on your feet. I have come to you to choose you to be my servant. You will tell people what you have seen of me today, and what I will show you later.
I will keep you safe from your own people and from the Gentiles. I am sending you to them

to open their eyes, so they will turn from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God. Then their sins will be forgiven, and they will have a place among God's people, who are made holy by believing in me.'
So, King Agrippa, I obeyed the vision from heaven.

First I preached to the people in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and in all of Judea, and also to the Gentiles. I told them to turn away from their sins and turn to God. I told them to show by what they do that they have really changed.
That is why the Jews grabbed me in the temple and tried to kill me.

But God has helped me to this very day. So I stand here and tell everyone, both important people and ordinary people, what I know. I say nothing more than what the prophets and Moses said would happen.
They said that the Christ would suffer and be the first to rise from the dead. They said he would bring the light of God to the Jews and to the Gentiles."
While Paul was still defending himself, Festus shouted, "Paul, you are out of your mind! Too much study has made you crazy!"
Paul answered, "I am not crazy, most excellent Festus. What I am saying is true and makes sense.
The king knows about these things, and I can speak freely to him. I am sure that he knows all about them, because these things did not happen in secret.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do."
Agrippa said to Paul, "Do you think you can make me a Christian so quickly?"
Paul answered, "Whether quickly or slowly, I pray to God that not only you but everyone listening to me today could become like me, except for these chains."
Then the king stood up, and so did the governor, Bernice, and the people sitting with them.
They left the room and talked to each other. They said, "This man has done nothing that deserves death or prison."
Agrippa said to Festus, "This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar."
